turns.prompt_text: How can I calibrate the compass on my phone?
turns.response_html:
Calibrating a smartphone compass is a straightforward process that relies on the device's internal magnetometer. Modern smartphones use a combination of GPS, Wi-Fi, and the magnetometer to determine your orientation and location.

The "Figure 8" Method

This is the universal standard for calibrating mobile sensors. It works by moving the phone through every possible three-dimensional orientation to help the sensor differentiate between the Earth's magnetic field and local interference.

  1. Open your Compass app or Google Maps.
  2. Hold your phone firmly in your hand.
  3. Move your phone through the air in a large, smooth figure-8 motion.
  4. While moving it, rotate your wrist so the phone tilts and flips slightly during the loops.
  5. Repeat this motion 3–5 times.

Calibration by Platform

On Android

If you are using Google Maps, there is a specific built-in tool to check your "Beam" (the blue shaded area pointing out from your location dot):

  • Open Google Maps.
  • Tap the blue dot that represents your location.
  • Tap Calibrate Compass at the bottom left.
  • Follow the on-screen instructions to tilt and move your phone. If the "Compass accuracy" says High, you’re good to go.

On iOS (iPhone)

Recent versions of iOS handle calibration automatically in the background, but you should ensure the settings are enabled:

  • Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services.
  • Scroll to the bottom and tap System Services.
  • Ensure Compass Calibration is toggled ON.
  • If the compass feels "stuck," simply opening the Compass app and performing the figure-8 motion usually resets it.

Pro-Tips for Accuracy

  • Avoid Magnets: Magnetic phone mounts, laptop speakers, or even magnetic clasps on phone cases can severely interfere with the sensor. Remove the case if the compass won't calibrate.
  • Stay Away from Metal: If you are standing next to a large steel structure (like a bridge or a car), the magnetometer may struggle. Move to an open area for the best results.
  • Check "True North": In your settings, you can usually toggle between True North (geographic) and Magnetic North. For general navigation, True North is typically preferred.

Does your compass seem to be drifting consistently in one direction, or is it jumping around randomly?

turns.prompt_text: I'm on a Google pixel 9. I'm not seeing the bottom left calibrate button
turns.response_html:
Ah, my bad—Google shifted that menu around on newer Pixel devices. It's actually tucked right into the main menu layout now rather than being its own standalone button in the corner.

On your Pixel 9, here is exactly where to look:

Finding Calibration on Pixel

  1. Open Google Maps and tap the blue dot showing your current location.
  2. A full-screen card titled "Your location" will slide up from the bottom.
  3. Look at the grid of circular quick-action buttons right below your address (usually things like Share location or Save parking).
  4. Swipe left across those circular buttons to reveal more options. You'll find Calibrate hidden right at the end of that row.

Once you tap it, you can choose between two methods:

  • Live View (Camera): This uses your camera to scan storefronts and street signs around you to instantly snap your orientation into place. It's incredibly fast if you are outdoors in a city.
  • Compass (Figure 8): If you're indoors or in a rural area, you can just tap the traditional compass option and do the tilt-and-rotate figure-8 motion shown in the image until the accuracy reading shifts to High.

Note: If the blue dot menu still isn't showing it, your compass sensor might actually already be at "High" accuracy. Google Maps occasionally hides the calibration prompt if it detects the sensor is perfectly stable.
